Lecture 38

Series solutions and the Frobenius method

We prove that at an ordinary point every solution is a power series whose radius is at least that of the coefficients, and we solve Legendre’s equation this way. At a regular singular point we derive the indicial equation, prove that the exponent with the larger real part gives a solution xαx^{\alpha}xα times a power series, and find a second solution, which may contain a logarithm when the exponents differ by a nonnegative integer.

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

  • Classify a point of a linear second-order equation as ordinary, regular singular or irregular singular.
  • Derive the recurrence for the coefficients and state the interval on which the series solves the equation.
  • Compute the indicial equation and its exponents, and construct a solution for the exponent with the larger real part.
  • Decide when a second solution may contain a logarithm, and construct it by reduction of order.

Lecture 7 solved Euler equations exactly and found second solutions by reduction of order. Most linear equations with variable coefficients have no solutions in closed form. The eigenvalue problems of Lectures 39 and 40 lead to Bessel’s and Legendre’s equations, whose coefficients are rational functions. In this lecture we construct the solutions of such equations as power series. The lecture reads in three stages: ordinary points and Legendre’s equation (Sections 38.1–38.2), Frobenius series at a regular singular point (Section 38.3), and the second solution when the exponents differ by an integer (Section 38.4).

Moreover, if ∑nanxn\sum_na_nx^n∑n​an​xn and ∑nbnxn\sum_nb_nx^n∑n​bn​xn have radii at least RRR, their product is (∑n=0∞anxn)(∑n=0∞bnxn)=∑n=0∞(∑k=0nakbn−k)xn(∣x∣<R),\Bigl(\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_nx^n\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_{n=0}^\infty b_nx^n\Bigr) =\sum_{n=0}^\infty\Bigl(\sum_{k=0}^na_kb_{n-k}\Bigr)x^n\qquad(\abs x<R),(n=0∑∞​an​xn)(n=0∑∞​bn​xn)=n=0∑∞​(k=0∑n​ak​bn−k​)xn(∣x∣<R),(38.2) with a radius at least RRR. Indeed, by Lecture 18’s proposition that power series are analytic, the two sums fff and ggg are analytic on the disc ∣z∣<R\abs z<R∣z∣<R in C\CC, so their product is analytic there. Lecture 18’s Taylor theorem expands the product in a power series with radius at least RRR, and its coefficients (fg)(n)(0)/n!(fg)^{(n)}(0)/n!(fg)(n)(0)/n! are the inner sums in (38.2), by the Leibniz rule (Lecture 21).

Summary

At an ordinary point every solution of y′′+Py′+Qy=0y''+Py'+Qy=0y′′+Py′+Qy=0 is a power series, and its radius is at least the radius of the series of PPP and QQQ, which complex singular points can limit. At a regular singular point the indicial equation gives two exponents. The exponent with the larger real part always gives a solution xα1x^{\alpha_1}xα1​ times a power series. The other exponent gives a second solution when the exponents do not differ by a nonnegative integer. Otherwise reduction of order gives a second solution that may contain y1ln⁡xy_1\ln xy1​lnx, and does when the exponents are equal.

  • Ordinary point: (n+2)(n+1)cn+2=−∑k≤n[(k+1)ck+1pn−k+ckqn−k](n+2)(n+1)c_{n+2}=-\sum_{k\le n}[(k+1)c_{k+1}p_{n-k}+c_kq_{n-k}](n+2)(n+1)cn+2​=−∑k≤n​[(k+1)ck+1​pn−k​+ck​qn−k​], radius at least that of PPP and QQQ.

  • Legendre: cn+2=(n−ℓ)(n+ℓ+1)cn/((n+1)(n+2))c_{n+2}=(n-\ell)(n+\ell+1)c_n/((n+1)(n+2))cn+2​=(n−ℓ)(n+ℓ+1)cn​/((n+1)(n+2)). A polynomial solution exists when ℓ\ellℓ is a nonnegative integer. Every series that does not terminate has the radius 111.

  • Indicial equation: F(α)=α(α−1)+p0α+q0=0F(\alpha)=\alpha(\alpha-1)+p_0\alpha+q_0=0F(α)=α(α−1)+p0​α+q0​=0, with xP=∑pnxnxP=\sum p_nx^nxP=∑pn​xn and x2Q=∑qnxnx^2Q=\sum q_nx^nx2Q=∑qn​xn.

  • Frobenius recurrence: F(α+n)cn=−∑k<n[(α+k)pn−k+qn−k]ckF(\alpha+n)c_n=-\sum_{k<n}[(\alpha+k)p_{n-k}+q_{n-k}]c_kF(α+n)cn​=−∑k<n​[(α+k)pn−k​+qn−k​]ck​, with F(α1+n)=n(n+α1−α2)F(\alpha_1+n)=n(n+\alpha_1-\alpha_2)F(α1​+n)=n(n+α1​−α2​).

  • Resonant case: α1−α2=m∈{0,1,2,…}\alpha_1-\alpha_2=m\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\}α1​−α2​=m∈{0,1,2,…} gives y2=xα2h2+c y1ln⁡xy_2=x^{\alpha_2}h_2+c\,y_1\ln xy2​=xα2​h2​+cy1​lnx, with c≠0c\ne0c=0 if m=0m=0m=0.

Lecture 39 applies the method to Bessel’s equation, whose point x=0x=0x=0 is a regular singular point.

References

Preparation: Lecture 7 (existence and uniqueness, the Wronskian test, reduction of order, Euler equations, Legendre’s equation with ℓ=1\ell=1ℓ=1), Lecture 18 (radius of convergence, power series are analytic, Taylor’s theorem, uniqueness of coefficients, the radius set by complex singular points); GM 29 (ratio test), GM 30 (integrated power series), GM 31 (termwise differentiation; exponential, sine, cosine and logarithm series).

Reading: G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems, AMS, 2012, §4.2; Riley, Hobson and Bence, Mathematical Methods for Physics and Engineering, 3rd ed., §§16.1–16.4.
